theme: Unit 18 review, The New Covenant Inaugurated, Mark
memoryText: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jesus says this to James and John, who have just asked for the best seats in his coming glory, and to the ten who are indignant. It is the key to the whole Gospel of Mark.

“For even the Son of Man.” The Son of Man is the figure of Daniel 7 who receives all authority and an everlasting kingdom. If anyone deserves to be served, it is he. The word “even” marks the surprise.

“Came not to be served.” He had every right to be served. He is the Lord of angels. Yet he refused to use his rights for himself. The King does not act like the kings of the Gentiles.

“But to serve.” The Servant King washes feet, feeds crowds, heals the sick, touches lepers, and welcomes children. His whole life was service.

“And to give his life.” Service reaches its height at the cross. His death was not a defeat but the purpose of his coming. He gave his life. No one took it from him.

“As a ransom for many.” A ransom is the price paid to free a prisoner. We were captive to sin, death, and the devil. The price was his life. The “many” means a multitude beyond number, all who trust him.

When you are tempted to seek your own greatness, say this verse. The greatest of all became the servant of all, and he did it for you.
unitRecap: You have read the Gospel of Mark, the fast-moving account of the servant King. It opened with the announcement that the kingdom of God is at hand, and showed Jesus acting with authority over demons, disease, nature, and death. Your doctrinal pause on the kingdom taught you to see it as already inaugurated and not yet complete. Along the way Jesus forgave sins, ate with sinners, taught in parables, and called his disciples to follow him. Again and again he silenced demons and those he healed, the so-called Messianic secret, because he would be known rightly only at the cross. At Caesarea Philippi, Peter finally confessed, “You are the Christ,” and Jesus began to teach that the Christ must suffer, be killed, and rise. The second half of the Gospel moves steadily toward Jerusalem: the Transfiguration, the passion predictions, the ransom saying of 10:45, Bartimaeus, the Entry, the temple controversies, and the Olivet Discourse. The passion narrative slows to a crawl: the anointing, the Supper, Gethsemane, the arrest, Peter’s denial, the silent King before Pilate, the cry of dereliction, and the torn curtain. A Roman centurion gave the Gospel’s climactic confession, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” And the Gospel ends at an empty tomb, with the message, “He has risen; he is not here.” Your Psalms carried the story: Psalm 107 on the stilling of the storm, Psalm 89 on David’s covenant, Psalm 118 on the rejected stone, and Psalm 69 on the righteous sufferer.
weekInReview: This week you read Psalm 118:19-29, the song of the rejected stone that became the cornerstone, and Psalm 69:1-21, the cry of the righteous sufferer whose thirst was met with sour wine. In Mark 14 you saw the woman anoint Jesus for burial, the Supper with its words about the body and the blood of the covenant, and the prayer in Gethsemane: “Abba, Father, yet not what I will, but what you will.” You watched Judas kiss him and the disciples flee. In chapters 14 and 15 you stood by as he was tried, denied by Peter, and flogged. You stood at the cross and heard the cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and saw the curtain torn in two. A Roman centurion confessed him as the Son of God. Finally, you came to the empty tomb and the announcement, “He has risen.”

reviewQuestions.question: What is the “Messianic secret” in Mark?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look at 1:25, 1:34, 1:44, 3:12, 5:43, 7:36, 8:30, and 9:9. Why do you think Jesus often commands silence? Consider how the cross changes what it means to call him the Christ, and write a few sentences.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does Mark’s Gospel move so quickly?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Notice the repeated “immediately” and the short, vivid scenes. What kind of Savior does that pace portray? What would it have meant for a suffering church in Rome to read this Gospel?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Mark’s Gospel build toward the cross as its climax?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Trace the three passion predictions (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34), the ransom saying in 10:45, and the proportion of the Gospel given to the final week. How does the centurion’s confession in 15:39 answer the question the Gospel has been asking?

reviewQuestions.question: What does Mark’s Passion narrative add to the other Gospels?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread chapters 14 and 15. Notice the starkness: the desertion by all the disciples, the single cry of dereliction, and the absence of any comfort. What do these details teach about the cost of the cross and about following Jesus?

prayerPrompts: Thank God for the Gospel of Mark and for the Servant who gave his life as a ransom.
Tell him what you have seen of Jesus.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
